headline: Your cartilage
body: Not your brain's clock. A clock inside the tissue.
punch: And a hormone in your bloodstream can reset it.

headline: Circadian rhythm
body: A master pacemaker in the brain telling the body what time it is. Peripheral tissues as passengers following instructions.
punch: Most tissues keep their own time.

headline: Cartilage
body: Growth plate cartilage runs a local circadian clock, measurable in organ-cultured femurs — isolated tissue, no brain attached, still keeping time.
punch: Disconnected from the body and still rhythmic.

headline: And PTH
body: Parathyroid hormone signalling resets the circadian clock specifically within cartilage — a previously uncharacterised link between PTH signalling and circadian biology in the growth plate.
punch: A hormone acting as a time signal, not just a growth signal.

headline: Why that's interesting
body: PTH and PTHrP already sit at the centre of growth plate regulation through the feedback loop controlling chondrocyte maturation. Now the same axis carries timing information.
punch: One pathway doing regulation and scheduling.

headline: Which raises
body: If the tissue's clock can be reset by a hormone, then sleep disruption, shift patterns and feeding timing all become plausible inputs to growth plate biology.
punch: Plausible. Not demonstrated — and that distinction is the point.

headline: This is where
body: A real mechanism gets discovered, and the sleep-optimisation version appears before anyone has measured a height outcome. The mechanism is real. The advice is invented.

headline: The honest position
body: Cartilage keeps local time and PTH can shift it. That's what's established. Everything downstream of it is currently a hypothesis wearing a lab coat.
punch: Knowing a clock exists isn't knowing how to set it.

headline: It's never over
body: Real mechanisms, real citations, no protocols.
